Key findings:
- 4‑year‑old with early, generalized severe loss of enamel and dentin, brown hard dentin, extreme attrition (surfaces worn to gingival level), exposed mandibular first molars and an associated abscess.
- Radiographs show obliterated pulp chambers in most teeth and constricted pulp chambers in others.

- No reported history of frequent fractures or other bone abnormalities (makes an osteogenesis imperfecta phenotype less likely but does not fully exclude variable expressivity).

Synthesis:
The combination of opalescent/brown discolored teeth, generalized rapid attrition with exposed dentin, and hallmark radiographic finding of obliterated pulp chambers is most characteristic of dentinogenesis imperfecta (DI), classically autosomal dominant and commonly due to DSPP mutations. DI frequently presents in primary dentition with amber/brown discoloration, early enamel fracture/attrition (because enamel fractures from abnormal underlying dentin), rapid wear down to gingival level, and radiographic obliteration of pulp chambers and canals from continued dentin deposition.

Differential considerations and why they are less likely:
- Dentin dysplasia (esp. type II) can present with discoloration and pulp anomalies in primary teeth (obliteration), but DI more typically produces the combination of brown opalescent teeth, severe attrition, and widespread obliteration described here. Dentin dysplasia often has more prominent root abnormalities and different radiographic pulp morphology in permanent teeth.
- Amelogenesis imperfecta (AI) affects enamel formation and causes enamel hypoplasia/hypomineralization and generalized wear, but radiographs in AI usually show normal pulp chambers unless severe secondary changes occur; AI does not explain the characteristic obliterated pulp chambers and brown dentin as well as DI does.
- Severe early childhood caries or environmental/erosive loss could produce generalized tooth substance loss and abscesses, but would be less likely to produce the familial, multi‑generation pattern or the radiographic pulp obliteration seen here.
- Dentin defects associated with osteogenesis imperfecta (DI type I) can present similarly; absence of a personal or family history of frequent fractures lowers the probability of OI, but mild OI phenotypes exist and should be considered and excluded because of management implications.

Most likely unifying diagnosis is an inherited dentin defect (dentinogenesis imperfecta spectrum), most consistent with DI type II (hereditary dentin defect without overt OI) in this pedigree.
